# Shared deployment — automatic publication disabled

As requested by the owner on 2026-10-30, GitHub Actions runs tests and build/artifact validation only. The `notify` job has been removed: main pushes do not send plugin.release_ready events, wait for an owner subscription, or publish the Site. Do not restore automatic publication or repository polling without an explicit owner request.

A successful GitHub workflow means source validation passed, not that production changed. For an explicitly requested deployment, verify the immutable GitHub commit and passing checks, preserve the existing shared Site and audience, reconcile existing source/provenance, build/package that source, and publish with native Sites tools. Report source commit, validation and production deployment separately. Existing secrets, event endpoint code and credentials are not modified by this workflow change.

## Historical event-driven deployment (inactive)

The configuration below documents the former integration and its provenance safeguards. It is not the active deployment policy. Missing subscriptions must not be worked around by automatically re-enabling them.

main push (from GitHub, a merged PR, or ChatGPT's connected GitHub tools) -> tests/build in GitHub Actions -> authenticated plugin.release_ready MCP event -> owner's ChatGPT Work cloud task -> publish the existing shared Site. All authorized Site viewers use the same running server. No repository polling schedule is used. The workflow only waits for the deployment it triggered.

One-time prerequisites: DEPLOY_OWNER_EMAIL set in Sites; one owner event subscription in ChatGPT Work; SITES_SERVICE_TOKEN stored only as a GitHub Actions secret. This service credential reaches the private Site gateway; the event endpoint additionally verifies the GitHub OIDC signature, repository ID, branch, workflow, event type and commit. It does not grant access to Sites source-management APIs. Never copy it into source or instructions.

The owner task must independently confirm the run's test job succeeded and current main matches the event SHA. Use connected GitHub tools and native Sites tools. Open the existing Sites source with a fresh short-lived source credential. Export exact tracked GitHub files at the immutable SHA (including hidden files, rejecting symlinks/submodules/credentials and incomplete trees), preserving storage and identity. Before publishing run Node tests, Python collector tests, build and artifact validation. Use pnpm frozen install if the dual lockfiles confuse the dependency helper.

Write .openai/github-release.json with {"repository":"kangjeongmin1229/f1-data-analyst","commit_sha":"<verified main SHA>"} into the Sites checkout before building. This is deployment provenance, not a user configuration change; do not commit it back to GitHub. Build embeds its SHA so Actions can verify the exact running release. Skip a duplicate only when a successful production deployment contains .openai/github-release.json with the exact event SHA. A bootstrap baseline matching source is only a comparison anchor and is not proof of release provenance; publish the provenance if it is absent. If main moved, do not deploy the obsolete event; the newer push has its own workflow. Record saved version/deployment IDs and resume them on retry instead of duplicating versions. Use shared save/deploy tools, preserving the current audience. Never use owner-private publication now that external viewers have access.

If existing Sites source contains unmirrored functional changes, stop and report the conflict rather than discard them. For subsequent deployments compare the saved github-release provenance and its GitHub source to current Sites files, ignoring only that generated provenance file and line endings. For the initial migration, the verified bootstrap correspondence is Site v19/source 0bdbe7a1144a87385fbd3ba7694a041284efe7ca and GitHub 26262afcb873b348c6709647b407b4b27d491425. Thereafter GitHub is authoritative. No automatic account-to-account cloning, no rights escalation, no secrets transfer to new viewers.

Failures in tests, subscription/authentication, callback delivery or cloud deployment fail the workflow or leave it awaiting explicit resolution; production is never intentionally replaced by an untested version. Event delivery has bounded retries and stable IDs. Re-running a failed workflow is the manual recovery path. Workflow and subscriber logs are the source of truth; event receipt alone is not deployment success.
